Prior distributions

Source: R/priors.R
prior_distributions.Rd

Constructors for the priors a tulpa_priors() specification takes, one per distribution:

  • prior_normal(): a normal prior.

  • prior_half_normal(): a half-normal prior (truncated at 0) for a positive parameter.

  • prior_half_cauchy(): a half-Cauchy prior for a positive parameter. It has heavier tails than the half-normal and is often used for variance parameters.

  • prior_gamma(): a gamma prior for a positive parameter.

  • prior_exponential(): an exponential prior for a positive parameter.

  • prior_beta(): a beta prior for a parameter bounded in (0, 1).

  • prior_pc(): a penalized complexity (PC) prior for a positive parameter, typically a standard deviation. PC priors shrink toward simpler models by penalizing deviation from a base model.

Usage

prior_normal(mean = 0, sd = 2.5)

prior_half_normal(sd = 1)

prior_half_cauchy(scale = 2.5)

prior_gamma(shape = 2, rate = 0.1)

prior_exponential(rate = 1)

prior_beta(alpha = 1, beta = 1)

prior_pc(U = 1, alpha = 0.01)

Arguments

mean

Prior mean of prior_normal(). Default 0.

sd

Standard deviation of prior_normal(), scale of prior_half_normal(). Must be positive.

scale

Scale of prior_half_cauchy(). Must be positive.

shape

Shape (alpha) of prior_gamma(). Must be positive.

rate

Rate of prior_gamma() (beta) or prior_exponential() (lambda). Must be positive.

alpha

First shape parameter of prior_beta(), or the tail probability of prior_pc(), P(x > U) = alpha (default 0.01). Must be positive; the tail probability must be below 1.

beta

Second shape parameter of prior_beta(). Must be positive.

U

Upper bound of prior_pc(): P(x > U) = alpha.

Value

A tulpa_prior object.

Details

The gamma prior has mean shape / rate and variance shape / rate^2.

The beta prior's shape parameters set its form:

  • alpha = beta = 1: Uniform(0, 1)

  • alpha = beta = 2: Symmetric, peaked at 0.5

  • alpha > beta: Skewed toward 1

  • alpha < beta: Skewed toward 0

The PC prior is specified via P(sigma > U) = alpha: U is the upper bound you consider "large" and alpha the probability of exceeding it. This implies an exponential prior with rate -log(alpha) / U.

References

Simpson, D., Rue, H., Riebler, A., Martins, T. G., & Sorbye, S. H. (2017). Penalising model component complexity: A principled, practical approach to constructing priors. Statistical Science, 32(1), 1-28.

Examples

prior_normal(0, 2.5)
#> Normal(0.00, 2.50)
prior_normal(0, 1)
#> Normal(0.00, 1.00)
prior_half_normal(1)
#> Half-Normal(1.00)
prior_half_cauchy(2.5)
#> Half-Cauchy(2.50)
prior_gamma(2, 0.1)  # Mean = 20, weakly informative
#> Gamma(2.00, 0.10)  [mean = 20.00]
prior_gamma(1, 1)    # Exponential(1)
#> Gamma(1.00, 1.00)  [mean = 1.00]
prior_exponential(1)
#> Exponential(1.00)  [mean = 1.00]
prior_beta(1, 1)   # Uniform
#> Beta(1.00, 1.00)  [mean = 0.50]
prior_beta(2, 2)   # Symmetric, centered at 0.5
#> Beta(2.00, 2.00)  [mean = 0.50]
prior_beta(5, 2)   # Skewed toward 1 (for high autocorrelation)
#> Beta(5.00, 2.00)  [mean = 0.71]
prior_pc(U = 1, alpha = 0.01)    # P(sigma > 1) = 0.01
#> PC prior: P(x > 1.00) = 0.010
#>   => Exponential(4.605)
prior_pc(U = 0.5, alpha = 0.05)  # Tighter, P(sigma > 0.5) = 0.05
#> PC prior: P(x > 0.50) = 0.050
#>   => Exponential(5.991)
